Today I'd like to look at why some volcanoes erupt explosively while others simply let lava pour out. The key factor is the viscosity of the magma, which is basically how thick and sticky it is. Magma that's low in silica, like what we see in Hawaii, is runny. Gas bubbles can rise through it and escape easily, so the lava flows out fairly gently. You can sometimes walk right up to the edge of a flow, though I wouldn't recommend it. Magma that's rich in silica is a different story. It's so thick that the gas can't get out. Pressure builds up, a bit like when you shake a bottle of soda with the cap on. When the pressure finally overcomes the rock above it, the magma shatters into ash and fragments, and you get an explosive eruption. Now, you might expect the amount of gas to be what matters most. And gas content is important, but two magmas with the same amount of gas can behave completely differently, depending on how easily that gas escapes. That's why volcanologists pay so much attention to silica content when they assess hazards. Next time, we'll look at what happens when magma meets groundwater, which can make even runny magma explosive.

Last week we talked about kinship terms, the words people use for their relatives. Today I want to show you how those terms can reveal the way a society is organized. In English, we use one word, cousin, for the children of all our parents' brothers and sisters. We don't distinguish between your mother's side and your father's side. But in many societies, that distinction is crucial. Take the system that anthropologists call Iroquois, named after the Native American nations where it was first described, though it's found all over the world. In this system, the children of your father's brother and of your mother's sister are called by the same terms as your own brothers and sisters. Only the children of your father's sister and of your mother's brother are what we would call cousins. So why would a society group relatives this way? One explanation is marriage rules. In many of these societies, you're expected to marry a cousin of the second type, but never one of the first type, since they count as siblings. So the vocabulary itself tells you who is a possible spouse. I should add that not everyone accepts this explanation, because some groups use these terms without any such marriage rules. Still, it's a useful reminder that kinship terms aren't just labels. They can carry social expectations.

Today, let's talk about green roofs. A green roof is a roof covered with soil and plants. Many cities are building them because summers are getting hotter. A normal dark roof gets very hot in the sun. But plants keep a roof cool, because they hold water and give off moisture into the air. This also helps the rooms below stay cooler, so people use less air conditioning. Green roofs help in another way, too. When it rains hard, the soil holds some of the water, so less water rushes into the streets at once. Green roofs cost more to build than normal roofs, but many cities think they are worth it.

In our anthropology class, we've been talking about families. In some cultures, a family means only parents and children. In others, a family is much larger. It can include grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins, all living in one house. Anthropologists call this an extended family. In an extended family, older people often help take care of the children while the parents work. In return, younger family members take care of the older ones when they get sick. Today, more people in many countries live in small families, often because they move to cities for jobs. But extended families are still common in many parts of the world.

When people talk about the printing revolution, they usually mean Gutenberg and the fourteen fifties. But East Asian printers had been using carved woodblocks for centuries, and movable type was invented in China around the ten forties, roughly four hundred years before Gutenberg. So the interesting question isn't who was first. It's why movable type transformed European publishing so quickly but remained, for a long time, a fairly minor technique in China. Part of the answer is the writing system itself. An alphabet needs only a few dozen letters, plus punctuation and capitals. A printer can cast thousands of copies of each and reuse them endlessly. Written Chinese, by contrast, uses thousands of distinct characters. A printer would need an enormous stock of type, and finding the right pieces could take longer than carving a whole new block. Woodblocks also had a practical advantage. Once a block was carved, it could be stored and used again years later, whenever demand for the book returned. With movable type, you'd break up the page after printing. Now, I don't want to suggest the technology was simply unsuitable. Korean printers used metal movable type quite successfully, and some Chinese projects used it on a large scale. The point is that the economics differed. For most Chinese publishers, woodblocks were the more sensible choice, not a backward one.

Let's continue with urban flooding. For most of the twentieth century, the dominant strategy was what engineers call gray infrastructure: pipes, concrete channels, and storm drains designed to move rainwater out of the city as fast as possible. The trouble is that these systems are sized for historical rainfall. When storms become more intense, as they are in many regions, the pipes simply overflow, and replacing them with larger ones is enormously expensive and disruptive. So a number of cities have taken a different approach, sometimes called the sponge city model. Instead of rushing water away, the idea is to slow it down and soak it up where it falls, using wetlands, permeable pavement that lets water seep through, and parks designed to flood temporarily. In Copenhagen, for instance, some public squares are built slightly below street level. On a normal day, they're basketball courts or plazas. During a cloudburst, they fill with water and then drain slowly. Now, I want to be careful here. Sponge features aren't a replacement for pipes. In dense city centers, there often isn't enough open land, and permeable surfaces can clog if they aren't maintained. Most planners see the two systems as complementary. The real shift is in the goal: not removing water from the city, but deciding where it can safely go.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Kinship Beyond Biology

Early anthropologists assumed that kinship everywhere was a cultural reflection of biological relatedness: people were related because they shared descent from a common ancestor. Fieldwork in the twentieth century complicated this view. Researchers found societies in which a child's relatives were determined only through the mother's line, so that a father belonged to a different kin group from his own children. Elsewhere, kinship could be created through everyday acts. In some communities, people who regularly shared food from the same hearth came to be regarded as kin, regardless of birth.

These findings led some scholars to argue that kinship is better understood as something people do rather than something they are born with. Critics of this position, however, caution against dismissing biology entirely. They note that even in societies where kinship can be acquired, ties traced through birth often carry obligations that acquired ties do not, such as rights to inherit land. The current consensus, if there is one, is that biology supplies the raw material, but each society decides which connections count, and how much.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Forecasting Eruptions

Volcanologists can rarely say exactly when a volcano will erupt, but they have become increasingly adept at recognizing the signs that one is restless. As magma ascends toward the surface, it fractures the surrounding rock, producing swarms of small earthquakes that seismometers can detect. The rising magma also releases dissolved gases, notably sulfur dioxide, whose concentration in the air above a vent often climbs in the weeks before an eruption. Meanwhile, satellite radar can register the swelling of a volcano's flanks by as little as a centimeter.

Yet these indicators are notoriously ambiguous. A volcano may display all of them and then subside without erupting, a phenomenon researchers call a failed eruption. Conversely, some eruptions have been preceded by only hours of detectable unrest. Because false alarms can erode public trust and impose heavy economic costs on evacuated communities, authorities are understandably reluctant to order evacuations on the basis of a single signal. Forecasters have therefore shifted from seeking a decisive warning sign toward probabilistic statements, estimating the likelihood of an eruption within a given period and revising that estimate as data accumulate.

email.title: Write an Email
email.subject: Cancelled evening class
email.prompt:
You recently joined your university's fitness center and paid for a semester membership that includes group classes. You chose this membership mainly for one evening class. However, that class has now been cancelled for the rest of the term, and the staff at the front desk could not answer your questions.

Write an email to the fitness center manager, Ms. Alvarez. In your email, do the following:
- Explain why you chose this membership.
- Describe the problem you have experienced.
- Ask what options are available to you.

Use full sentences, and write as much as you can.
email.rubric: Task: polite complaint and request email to a manager. Must cover all 3 bullets: (1) reason for choosing the membership (the evening class, schedule, cost, etc.), (2) clear description of the problem (class cancelled, front desk could not help), (3) a specific question about options (refund, transfer, other class, partial credit). Look for appropriate register (polite, firm, not rude), greeting and sign-off, logical order, accurate grammar, varied and precise vocabulary. Typical strong length 100-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt:
Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, do these two things.
- State your view and back it up.
- Add something new to the thread, in your own words.
Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Lindqvist
professor.text: As summers become hotter and storms stronger, cities must decide how to spend limited money on adapting to climate change. Some planners argue that cities should invest mainly in large engineering projects, such as sea walls and bigger drainage systems, because these protect many people at once. Others argue that the money is better spent on many small, local measures, such as planting street trees, building green roofs and opening cooling centers in neighborhoods. Which approach should cities give priority to, and why?

students.name: Hana
students.text: I think large projects should come first. A single flood can destroy thousands of homes, and trees or green roofs cannot stop a storm surge. Small measures are nice, but they are not enough when the danger is serious.

students.name: Mateo
students.text: I prefer small local measures. Big projects take decades to plan and build, while trees and cooling centers help people this summer. They also spread the benefits across many neighborhoods instead of only the areas near the coast.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear opinion on which approach to prioritize, specific reasons or examples (cost, speed, scale of risk, fairness between neighborhoods), engagement with Hana's or Mateo's point that adds something new rather than repeating it, coherence, and varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.

interview.instructions: An interviewer will ask you four questions. There is no preparation time. You have 45 seconds to answer each question.
interview.context: You are joining a research study about reading habits. A researcher will ask you some questions in a short online interview.

items.text: Thank you for joining this study about how people read. To begin, could you tell me what kinds of things you usually read in a typical week?
Some people prefer printed books, while others prefer reading on a screen. Which do you prefer, and why?
Some people believe that reading on screens has made it harder for people to concentrate on long texts. Do you agree or disagree? Please explain.
Let me ask one last question. Some libraries are reducing their collections of printed books to create more space for computers and group study. Do you think this is a good decision? Why or why not?
